title: The sand mandala
hook: monks build a palace of colored sand grain by grain, and then sweep it into a jar

segments.voice: Yesterday, the teacher and lineage: the reading aloud, the empowerment, the chain of people. Your line was some things need a teacher. Did you thank someone who taught you? Today, something monks make together, and then unmake. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-eight.

A low square table in a museum lobby. Around it, a few Tibetan monks lean in so close their noses nearly touch the surface. Each holds a thin metal funnel and rubs a rod along its ridged side, and the vibration lets out colored sand, a few grains at a time. A thin blue line. A red petal. A gold edge. Visitors come back day after day to watch the circle grow, more detailed than seems possible. And then, at the end, the monks chant, pick up brushes, and sweep the whole thing from the edges into the center. A gray-brown pile. A jar. Today's word is that circle, and what happens to it.
screen: `A FUNNEL. A FEW GRAINS.` → `THE CIRCLE GROWS.` → `THEN THE BRUSHES COME OUT.`

segments.voice: Mandala is a Sanskrit word for a circle. In Tibetan Buddhism a mandala is a picture of an awakened world, often drawn as a palace seen from above, with a buddha or deity at the center and gates opening in each direction. Four turns. First, it's a map, not a decoration. Every color, symbol and line has a meaning in the practice it belongs to. A sand mandala is usually made for a particular ceremony, and those who use it in practice learn to visualize the palace in their minds. Second, the making is itself practice. The monks work with chanting and concentration, grain by grain. A shaky hand or a sneeze can undo an hour. Patience isn't a side effect. It's part of the offering. Third, the sweep. When the ceremony is done, the mandala is dismantled on purpose, with prayers. The sand is gathered up, some of it is given to people watching as a blessing, and the rest is often carried to a river or other flowing water and poured in, so the blessing travels on. Fourth, why sweep it at all? Buddhist teaching holds that everything made of parts comes apart: the word for this is impermanence. Teachers use the sweep to make that teaching visible. All that skill, all that beauty, and the hand that made it is the hand that clears it away. The surprise, for some watching, is that the sweeping doesn't look like a loss. It looks like the last step of the work.
screen: `A PALACE SEEN FROM ABOVE.` · `THE MAKING IS PRACTICE.` · `SWEPT UP, POURED INTO WATER.` · `EVERYTHING MADE COMES APART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make something and let it go. Gather a few small things within reach: coins, pens, keys, a leaf, a cup. Slowly arrange them into a small pattern, a circle if you like, with a center. Take care with it. Move one thing a little to the left. Look at it. Then, with the same care, gather it all back up, one piece at a time, and put each thing where it came from. Notice what the letting go feels like in your hands. The bell holds the time.
The sand mandala. A Tibetan picture of an awakened world, built grain by grain for a ceremony, and then swept away to show that everything made comes apart. Today's word.

Your line: sweep it away. Today, when you finish something, a clean counter, a sent message, a finished meal, let it be finished, without looking back to admire or fix it. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Tibetan monks make sand mandalas for particular ceremonies, working with chanting and fine metal funnels, and when the ceremony ends they dismantle the mandala with prayers, sharing some sand and pouring the rest into flowing water.
